explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a psychrophile that can grow at refrigerator temperatures (4°C), enabling it to contaminate refrigerated foods.
Saliva contains the highest concentration of rabies virus; a skin biopsy from the nape of the neck (hair follicles) is also used for fluorescent antibody testing.
Dronabinol (synthetic THC) is used medically for cannabis dependence, providing agonist effects that reduce withdrawal and craving.
The urea cycle releases urea and fumarate; fumarate enters the citric acid cycle, linking the two cycles at the argininosuccinate step.
PNMT (phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase) converts norepinephrine to epinephrine and is induced by cortisol in the adrenal medulla.
Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine; BH4 deficiency causes PKU.
Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine with characteristic sweet odor.
TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is the coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids including pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and branched-chain ketoacids.
Pellagra results from niacin (B3) deficiency, classically presenting with the 4 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated.
Folate (as N5, N10-methylene-THF) donates one-carbon units in purine synthesis and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis.
Methyl-THF transfers its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
Amino acid catabolism releases free ammonia via transamination and oxidative deamination; this ammonia is converted to urea for excretion.
ADP and GDP are allosteric activators of glutamate dehydrogenase, which catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate.
N-acetylglutamate (synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate) is the essential allosteric activator of CPS I, the first urea cycle enzyme.
Fumarate links the urea and citric acid cycles; it is produced from argininosuccinate in the urea cycle and enters the CAC.
Serotonin (5-HT) is synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase (rate-limiting) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase.
The CNS is soft because it lacks connective tissue framework; neurons and glia are supported primarily by neuroglial cells, not connective tissue.
The blood-CSF barrier uses fenestrated endothelial cells (allowing passage) and is NOT formed by astrocyte foot processes (those form the BBB).
Right cerebral peduncle lesion causes left-sided motor weakness (contralateral) because corticospinal fibers have already crossed at the pyramidal decussation.
Golgi tendon organs (type Ib) detect muscle tension and trigger inverse stretch reflex causing sudden muscle relaxation when tension becomes dangerous.
The spinal cord has cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3) enlargements for limb innervation, corresponding to brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.
In adults the spinal cord extends from C1 to L1 vertebra, while in newborns it extends from C1 to L3 vertebra due to differential vertebral column growth.
modelAnswer: Adult: C1 till L1; Newborn: C1 till L3.

explanation: The three ligaments supporting the spinal cord are the filum terminale (coccygeal ligament), ligamentum denticulatum, and subarachnoid septum.
modelAnswer: Filum terminale, ligamentum denticulatum, subarachnoid septum.

explanation: The dura mater and arachnoid mater (the meninges) end opposite the S2 vertebra, forming the sacral dural sac.
modelAnswer: mater and arachnoid mater end opposite which vertebrae? S2

explanation: The scalp extends from the supraorbital margin anteriorly to the external occipital protuberance posteriorly, and to the superior temporal line laterally.
modelAnswer: Anteriorly: supraorbital margin; Posteriorly: external occipital protuberance and highest nuchal line; Laterally: superior temporal line.

explanation: Dense connective tissue in the scalp means infections remain localized, wounds gape less due to fibrous septa, and small wounds cause profuse bleeding from arteries.
modelAnswer: Infection remains localized, wounds don't gap, small wound causes profuse bleeding.

explanation: The frontal belly of occipitofrontalis is innervated by the temporal branch of facial nerve; the occipital belly is innervated by the posterior auricular branch.
modelAnswer: Frontal belly: temporal branch of facial nerve; Occipital belly: posterior auricular branch of facial nerve.

explanation: The loose areolar tissue (dangerous layer) contains valveless emissary veins connecting scalp veins to intracranial venous sinuses, allowing infection spread.
modelAnswer: Because its emissary veins can spread infection from scalp to cranial cavity.

explanation: Anterior to auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal nerves; posterior to auricle: great auricular, lesser/greater occipital, third occipital.
modelAnswer: In front of auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal; Behind auricle: great auricular, lesser occipital, greater occipital, third occipital.

explanation: The face is bounded superiorly by the hairline, inferiorly by the lower mandibular border, and laterally by the auricles connecting both sides.
modelAnswer: Superior: hair line; Inferior: lower border of mandible; Sideways: from one auricle to the other.

explanation: The facial artery terminates by anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery, completing the arterial supply around the eye and nose.
The two terminal branches of the facial artery within the face are the superior labial artery and inferior labial artery supplying the lips.
The anterior facial vein communicates deeply with the superior ophthalmic vein (to cavernous sinus) and deep facial vein (to pterygoid plexus).
modelAnswer: To superior ophthalmic vein (→ cavernous sinus) and to deep facial vein (→ pterygoid venous plexus → cavernous sinus via emissary veins).

explanation: The dangerous area of the face (midline triangle including upper lip and nose) connects via angular/emissary veins to the cavernous sinus.
modelAnswer: Triangle including upper lip, nose, medial angles of eye. Infection can spread to cavernous sinus causing thrombosis.

explanation: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches in the face include supratrochlear, supraorbital (from frontal nerve), and infratrochlear nerves.
modelAnswer: Supratrochlear, supraorbital, palpebral branch of lacrimal, infratrochlear.
